options: every one of its points is an interior point
questions.explanation: Open means the set equals its interior: around every point of the set there is some ball, of positive radius, that stays inside the set. Containing the boundary is the extra demand that makes a set closed, and an open ball does not contain its sphere. Boundedness and the origin are irrelevant. The whole space is open, and so is the empty set.

questions.prompt: What is the largest radius of an open ball about \((2, 0)\) that sits inside the open ball of radius 7 about the origin?
questions.explanation: The center \((2, 0)\) is at distance 2 from the origin, and the outer radius is 7, so the gap is \(7 - 2 = 5\). Any point within distance strictly less than 5 of \((2, 0)\) has norm strictly less than 7, by the triangle inequality. A larger test radius reaches the sphere or beyond it. The distance 2 alone is the distance to the origin, not the room that remains.

questions.prompt: The closed unit ball \(\{x : \lVert x \rVert_2 \le 1\}\) is
questions.explanation: The inequality is not strict, so the sphere is included and the set contains its boundary. It is closed. A point on the sphere has no ball that stays inside the set, because every ball around it leaves the unit ball. It is not open. The empty set and the whole space are the usual sets that are both. An open ball, with a strict inequality, is the set that is open and not closed.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show that a point \(x\) with \(\lVert x \rVert < R\) is an interior point of the open ball of radius \(R\).
questions.explanation: The gap \(R - \lVert x \rVert\) is positive exactly because \(x\) is inside the open ball. That gap is the largest test radius that works. The triangle inequality then says \(\lVert y \rVert \le \lVert y - x \rVert + \lVert x \rVert\), and a strict inequality in the test ball keeps \(\lVert y \rVert < R\). Starting from the triangle inequality before the gap is known does not produce a radius. Using a nonpositive radius would not show an interior point.

questions.figure_alt: A filled disk centered at the origin.
steps: Subtract \(\lVert x \rVert\) from \(R\) to get a positive gap.
Use that gap as the radius of a test ball about \(x\).
For a point \(y\) of the test ball, bound \(\lVert y \rVert\) by the triangle inequality.
Check that the bound is strictly less than \(R\), so the test ball lies in the open ball.

questions.prompt: In \(\mathbb{R}\), what is the largest radius of an open ball about 4 that lies in the open interval \((1, 8)\)?
questions.explanation: The distance from 4 to 1 is 3, and the distance from 4 to 8 is 4. The limiting endpoint is the nearer one, so the largest radius is 3. Any open interval of that radius about 4 stays inside \((1, 8)\). The radius 4 would reach 0, which is outside the interval. The length of \((1, 8)\) is 7, which is not the room around the point 4.

questions.prompt: In \(\mathbb{R}\), how many points does the closure of the set \(\{1, 1/2, 1/3\}\) contain?
questions.explanation: The set already has the three points 1, \(1/2\), and \(1/3\). The sequence approaches 0, and 0 is not one of the three, so the closure adds 0 and contains 4 points. Counting only the original three misses the limit. Counting only 0 would replace the set by its missing limit instead of adding that limit.

questions.prompt: Which of these subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^2\) are open?
questions.explanation: The open disk of radius 2 is open by the ball definition, and the strict half-plane \(x_1 > 0\) is open because a point with first coordinate \(c > 0\) has a ball of radius \(c\) that stays in the half-plane. The closed disk includes its circle, and those boundary points are not interior. A singleton in \(\mathbb{R}^2\) has empty interior: every ball around the origin contains other points.

questions.prompt: What is the largest radius of an open ball about \((0, 4)\) that lies in the open half-plane \(\{x : x_2 > 0\}\)?
questions.explanation: The point is 4 units above the boundary line \(x_2 = 0\). A ball of radius 4 stays strictly above that line, and any larger ball crosses it or touches it. The first coordinate is 0, which is not a distance to the boundary. Twice the height, 8, would be the width of a ball that is already too big.

questions.prompt: One of these steps is false. Select that step, and the reason it fails.
questions.explanation: The point on the sphere does lie in the closed ball, and every ball around it does meet the closed ball. The last step only applies the test stated just above it. That test is false. An interior point needs some ball that lies entirely inside the set, not a ball that merely meets the set. Every ball around a sphere point also meets the complement, so x is a boundary point. The radius of those balls is positive; that is not what failed. The closed ball is not empty.

steps: Let C be the closed unit ball, and let x be a point of C on the unit sphere.
Every ball around x meets C.
A point of C is interior whenever every ball around it meets C.
Applying that test to x says that x is an interior point of C.
reasons: Meeting the set is not enough for an interior point. A ball around this x always leaves C.
The ball around x was required to have radius zero, so the step never tested a neighborhood.
A closed ball is empty, so it has no point of norm 1.

questions.prompt: The open unit ball in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) fails to be compact because
options: it does not contain its boundary
questions.explanation: The open unit ball is bounded, nonempty, and convex. It leaves out the unit sphere, so it is not closed. In \(\mathbb{R}^n\) a compact set has to be closed and bounded, and the missing boundary is the property that fails. That is the fact a later compactness test spends.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood used to define a local minimizer is an open ball. The point \((1, 2)\) lies in the open ball of radius 3 about the origin. What is the squared Euclidean distance from \((1, 2)\) to the origin?
questions.explanation: The squared distance is \(1^2 + 2^2 = 5\). The distance itself is \(\sqrt{5}\), which is less than 3, so the point really is inside that neighborhood. The sum of the coordinates is 3, and the product is 2. Neither is the squared length. Neighborhoods in a local-minimum definition are open sets of this kind.

questions.prompt: Which of these sets is both open and closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)?
options: a line in the plane, when \(n = 2\)
questions.explanation: The whole space has empty boundary, so it contains its boundary and every point is interior. It is closed and open. The empty set is the other usual example. An open ball misses its sphere. A singleton and a line in the plane are closed and have empty interior, so they are not open. A closed set that is not compact, such as the whole space, is exactly why a later existence argument asks for something smaller than closedness alone.
